claim: RbpA is essential in mycobacteria.

evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Forti et al., 2011; Stallings and Glickman, 2011; Tabib-Salazar et al., 2013).

claim: Mycobacterial holoenzyme forms an unstable RPo with a half-life of a few minutes or less compared with E. coli holoenzyme on the same promoters.
source: In contrast to Eco holo, which forms an essentially irreversible RPo on many promoters, the mycobacterial holo forms an unstable RPo with a half-life of a few minutes or less when compared with Eco holo on the same promoters (Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Davis et al., 2015).

claim: E. coli holoenzyme forms an essentially irreversible RPo on many promoters.
source: In contrast to Eco holo, which forms an essentially irreversible RPo on many promoters, the mycobacterial holo forms an unstable RPo with a half-life of a few minutes or less when compared with Eco holo on the same promoters (Davis et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Davis et al., 2015).

claim: CarD associates with RNAP through its interaction with β-lobe 1.
source: CarD associates with RNAP through its interaction with β-lobe 1 (also known as the protrusion; Bae et al., 2015a; Stallings et al., 2009) and stabilizes RPo by wedging a conserved Trp residue into the widened minor groove at the upstream edge of the transcription bubble (Bae et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bae et al., 2015a; Stallings et al., 2009).

claim: CarD stabilizes RPo by wedging a conserved Trp residue into the widened minor groove at the upstream edge of the transcription bubble.
source: CarD associates with RNAP through its interaction with β-lobe 1 (also known as the protrusion; Bae et al., 2015a; Stallings et al., 2009) and stabilizes RPo by wedging a conserved Trp residue into the widened minor groove at the upstream edge of the transcription bubble (Bae et al., 2015a).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Bae et al., 2015a).

claim: RbpA forms a tight interaction with the σ2 domain of Group 1 and Group 2 σ factors through its C-terminal σ-interacting domain (SID).
source: RbpA forms a tight interaction with the σ2 domain (−10 element recognition domain) of Group 1 and Group 2 σ factors through its C-terminal σ-interacting domain (SID; Bortoluzzi et al., 2013; Hubin et al., 2015; Tabib-Salazar et al., 2013), but how other RbpA structural elements interact with the transcription initiation complex (TIC) and activate transcription is unknown.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bortoluzzi et al., 2013; Hubin et al., 2015; Tabib-Salazar et al., 2013).

claim: CarD is present at most, if not all, σA promoters in mycobacteria.
source: ChIP-Seq studies indicate CarD is present at most, if not all, σA promoters in mycobacteria (Srivastava et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Srivastava et al., 2013).

claim: RbpA forms a very tight complex with σA and σA-holo.
source: Comprehensive genomic data for RbpA occupancy in vivo is not available, but RbpA forms a very tight complex with σA and σA-holo (Hubin et al., 2015) and is likely present at most σA promoters as well.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hubin et al., 2015).

claim: RbpA is likely present at most σA promoters.
source: Comprehensive genomic data for RbpA occupancy in vivo is not available, but RbpA forms a very tight complex with σA and σA-holo (Hubin et al., 2015) and is likely present at most σA promoters as well.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the tight binding of RbpA to σA and σA-holo, though comprehensive genomic data is not available.

claim: RbpA and CarD cooperatively stimulate formation of an intermediate (RP2) leading to RPo.
source: Mechanistic analyses of promoter open complex (RPo) formation establish that RbpA and CarD cooperatively stimulate formation of an intermediate (RP2) leading to RPo; formation of RP2 is likely a bottleneck step at the majority of mycobacterial promoters.
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanistic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Formation of RP2 is likely a bottleneck step at the majority of mycobacterial promoters.
source: Mechanistic analyses of promoter open complex (RPo) formation establish that RbpA and CarD cooperatively stimulate formation of an intermediate (RP2) leading to RPo; formation of RP2 is likely a bottleneck step at the majority of mycobacterial promoters.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mechanistic analyses and the observation that most mycobacterial promoters lack a -35 element.

claim: CarD disfavors isomerization of RPo back to RP2 once RPo forms.
source: Once RPo forms, CarD also disfavors its isomerization back to RP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by mechanistic analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: A 2.76 Å-resolution crystal structure of a mycobacterial transcription initiation complex (TIC) with RbpA was determined.
source: We determined a 2.76 Å-resolution crystal structure of a mycobacterial transcription initiation complex (TIC) with RbpA as well as a CarD/RbpA/TIC model.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure determination described in the manuscript.

claim: A CarD/RbpA/TIC model was determined.
source: We determined a 2.76 Å-resolution crystal structure of a mycobacterial transcription initiation complex (TIC) with RbpA as well as a CarD/RbpA/TIC model.
evidence: The claim is supported by the structural modeling described in the manuscript.

claim: Both CarD and RbpA bind near the upstream edge of the −10 element.
source: Both CarD and RbpA bind near the upstream edge of the −10 element where they likely facilitate DNA bending and impede transcription bubble collapse.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure and structural modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: CarD and RbpA likely facilitate DNA bending.
source: Both CarD and RbpA bind near the upstream edge of the −10 element where they likely facilitate DNA bending and impede transcription bubble collapse.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural positions of CarD and RbpA and their effects on transcription.

claim: CarD and RbpA likely impede transcription bubble collapse.

evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural positions of CarD and RbpA and their effects on RPo stability.

claim: In vivo studies demonstrate the essential role of RbpA.
source: In vivo studies demonstrate the essential role of RbpA, show the effects of RbpA truncations on transcription and cell physiology, and indicate additional functions for RbpA not evident in vitro.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RbpA truncations affect transcription and cell physiology in vivo.
source: In vivo studies demonstrate the essential role of RbpA, show the effects of RbpA truncations on transcription and cell physiology, and indicate additional functions for RbpA not evident in vitro.

claim: RbpA has additional functions not evident in vitro.
source: In vivo studies demonstrate the essential role of RbpA, show the effects of RbpA truncations on transcription and cell physiology, and indicate additional functions for RbpA not evident in vitro.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis is the causative agent of tuberculosis.
source: The bacterial pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) is the causative agent of tuberculosis, an ongoing world health problem.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge.

claim: RNA polymerase is the target of the rifamycin class of antibiotics.
source: RNA polymerase (RNAP), responsible for all transcription in bacteria, is the target of the rifamycin class of antibiotics, a first-line therapeutic treatment for tuberculosis (Chakraborty and Rhee, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Chakraborty and Rhee, 2015).

claim: Rifamycins are a first-line therapeutic treatment for tuberculosis.

claim: RNAP is a proven drug target.
source: Thus, RNAP is a proven drug target, highlighting the importance of gaining a structural and functional understanding of mycobacterial transcription - an understanding made difficult by the lack of a mycobacterial RNAP structure.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the fact that rifamycins target RNAP and are used clinically.

claim: Bacterial transcription initiation is controlled by promoter-specificity σ-factors.
source: Bacterial transcription initiation is controlled by promoter-specificity σ-factors, which associate with the core RNAP (α2ββ'ω subunits), generating the holoenzyme (holo; Gruber and Gross, 2003; Murakami and Darst, 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gruber and Gross, 2003; Murakami and Darst, 2003).

claim: σ-factors associate with core RNAP to generate the holoenzyme.

claim: Promoter DNA sequences are recognized by holoenzyme.
source: Promoter DNA sequences are recognized by holo (Murakami et al., 2002), triggering a series of conformational changes as the enzyme unwinds 12 to 14 base pairs of DNA to generate the transcription bubble and loads the template-strand (t-strand) DNA into the RNAP active site, resulting in the transcriptionally-competent open promoter complex (RPo; Saecker et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Murakami et al., 2002).

claim: Holoenzyme unwinds 12 to 14 base pairs of DNA to generate the transcription bubble.

claim: The combination of RbpA with CarD had a strongly cooperative effect, extending RPo half-life more than 2-fold compared to CarD alone.

source: A sequential mechanism involving at least three steps has been proposed for Eco σ70-holo based on several decades of studies using the lacUV5 (Buc and McClure, 1985), λPR (Roe et al., 1985; Saecker et al., 2011), T7A1 (Sclavi et al., 2005), and rrnB P1 (Rutherford et al., 2009) promoters:
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Buc and McClure, 1985; Roe et al., 1985; Saecker et al., 2011; Sclavi et al., 2005; Rutherford et al., 2009).

evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Saecker et al., 2011).

claim: The three-step sequential model best accounted for all of the kinetic data.
source: We analyzed the fluorescence progress curves (Figure 3A–C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C) by globally fitting the data for each concentration series collected on a given day to a kinetic mechanism (Johnson et al., 2009b, 2009a). We assumed that the different RNAPs (Eco or Mbo) or presence of the factors determined the rate constants associated with the mechanism, but did not alter the basic mechanism. Based on previous analyses (Buc and McClure, 1985; Roe et al., 1985; Rutherford et al., 2009; Saecker et al., 2011; Sclavi et al., 2005), we considered sequential (linear) kinetic schemes (Appendix). The three-step sequential model best accounted for all of the kinetic data (Supplementary file 4, Appendix), consistent with previous work with Eco RNAP.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis of fluorescence data.

claim: The three-step sequential model for mycobacterial RNAP is consistent with previous work with E. coli RNAP.
source: The three-step sequential model best accounted for all of the kinetic data (Supplementary file 4, Appendix), consistent with previous work with Eco RNAP.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with published literature on E. coli RNAP.

claim: The rate-limiting step in the forward direction is the conversion of RP2 -> RPo on the AP3 promoter.
source: Analysis of the activation energies required to traverse the transition states for each kinetic step indicates that for all of the samples on the AP3 promoter, the rate-limiting step (the highest activation energy) in the forward direction is the conversion of RP2 -> RPo, while the same step is rate-limiting in the reverse direction (RPo -> RP2; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by activation energy analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The rate-limiting step in the reverse direction is the conversion of RPo -> RP2 on the AP3 promoter.
source: Analysis of the activation energies required to traverse the transition states for each kinetic step indicates that for all of the samples on the AP3 promoter, the rate-limiting step (the highest activation energy) in the forward direction is the conversion of RP2 -> RPo, while the same step is rate-limiting in the reverse direction (RPo -> RP2; Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by activation energy analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The rate-limiting RP2 -> RPo step corresponds to the formation of the full transcription bubble.
source: Consistent with previous analyses, we hypothesized that this rate-limiting step in the forward direction corresponds to the formation of the full transcription bubble (Saecker et al., 2011). We tested this hypothesis by monitoring the time-dependent fluorescence from an AP3 promoter derivative harboring 2-aminopurine (2-AP) at the t-strand +2 position (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G) during RPo formation.
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-AP fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 3D-E and a citation to published literature (Saecker et al., 2011).

claim: An increase of 2-AP fluorescence signals full transcription bubble formation.
source: We placed 2-AP at the very downstream edge of the transcription bubble so that an increase of 2-AP fluorescence signals full transcription bubble formation, directly preceding or concurrent with RPo formation.
evidence: The claim is based on the known properties of 2-AP fluorescence and its placement in the promoter.

claim: The apparent rate constant for 2-AP AP3 fluorescence increase (kappexp = 0.030 s−1) is nearly identical to the rate of RPo formation simulated from the independently determined kinetic parameters (kappsim = 0.034 s−1).
source: We fit the data to a single-exponential to obtain an apparent rate constant, kappexp = 0.030 s−1 (Figure 3D), nearly identical to the rate of RPo formation simulated from the independently determined kinetic parameters (Table 1; Figure 3E; kappsim = 0.034 s−1), suggesting that the rate-limiting RP2 -> RPo transition involves the formation of the full transcription bubble.
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-AP fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: The rate-limiting RP2 -> RPo transition involves the formation of the full transcription bubble.
source: We fit the data to a single-exponential to obtain an apparent rate constant, kappexp = 0.030 s−1 (Figure 3D), nearly identical to the rate of RPo formation simulated from the independently determined kinetic parameters (Table 1; Figure 3E; kappsim = 0.034 s−1), suggesting that the rate-limiting RP2 -> RPo transition involves the formation of the full transcription bubble.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the agreement between 2-AP fluorescence kinetics and simulated RPo formation kinetics.

claim: RbpA has a more potent effect on transcription of the Mtb VapB promoter than on AP3.
source: It has been noted that RbpA has a more potent effect on transcription of the Mtb VapB promoter than on AP3 (Hubin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Hubin et al., 2015).

claim: M. bovis holo forms RPo on VapB about 10 times more slowly than on AP3.
source: Mbo holo forms RPo on VapB about 10 times more slowly than on AP3 (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The VapB kinetic data were best fit by the sequential three-step model.
source: The VapB kinetic data were also best fit by the sequential three-step model (Equation 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis of VapB fluorescence data.

claim: The RP1 -> RP2 transition (k2) is much slower on VapB compared to AP3.
source: When comparing Mbo holo, Mbo holo+RbpA, and Eco holo on the two promoters, the consistently significant difference in the kinetic parameters is that the RP1 -> RP2 transition (k2) is much slower on VapB; the VapB k2 is 7-fold (Mbo holo+RbpA), 47-fold (Mbo holo alone), or 230-fold (Eco holo) smaller than the AP3 k2 (Supplementary file 6; Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in Supplementary file 6 and Figure 4B.

claim: RbpA targets the RP1 -> RP2 transition, increasing k2 on VapB by more than 20-fold.
source: Like on AP3 (Table 1; Figure 3F), RbpA targets the RP1 -> RP2 transition, increasing k2 on VapB by more than 20-fold (Supplementary file 6; Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in Supplementary file 6 and Figure 4C.

claim: Full-length RbpA is essential for normal growth of M. smegmatis.
source: The increased in vitro activity of RbpASID-BL (Figure 2B–C) led us to investigate whether the NTT and CD were required for the essential functions of RbpA in vivo.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: rbpA is essential in mycobacteria.
source: As rbpA was previously shown to be essential in mycobacteria (Bortoluzzi et al., 2013; Forti et al., 2011; Sassetti et al., 2003), we generated a ΔrbpA allele in a strain carrying a second copy of rbpA integrated at the attB chromosomal site conferring streptomycin resistance (MGM6228), which can be efficiently swapped for rbpA alleles on an attB integrating plasmid conferring kanamycin resistance.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bortoluzzi et al., 2013; Forti et al., 2011; Sassetti et al., 2003).

claim: Swapping a vector control plasmid for rbpA yielded no transformants.
source: In accordance with the essential role of rbpA, swapping a vector control plasmid for rbpA yielded no transformants, in contrast to efficient marker exchange seen with full length RbpA.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RbpACD-BL-SID, RbpABL-SID, and RbpAR79A all supported viability.
source: We next tested rbpA mutant alleles encoding the RbpA derivatives tested in vitro (Figure 2A). RbpACD-BL-SID, RbpABL-SID, and RbpAR79A all supported viability.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RbpAwt doubled at 2.6(±0.16) hr.
source: Whereas RbpAwt doubled at 2.6(±0.16) hr, RbpACD-BL-SID doubled slightly slower at 3.13(±0.16) hr and RbpABL-SID and RbpAR79A doubled even more slowly at 4.1(±0.21) hr and 4.6(±0.96) hr, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RbpACD-BL-SID doubled at 3.13(±0.16) hr.
source: Whereas RbpAwt doubled at 2.6(±0.16) hr, RbpACD-BL-SID doubled slightly slower at 3.13(±0.16) hr and RbpABL-SID and RbpAR79A doubled even more slowly at 4.1(±0.21) hr and 4.6(±0.96) hr, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RbpABL-SID doubled at 4.1(±0.21) hr.
source: Whereas RbpAwt doubled at 2.6(±0.16) hr, RbpACD-BL-SID doubled slightly slower at 3.13(±0.16) hr and RbpABL-SID and RbpAR79A doubled even more slowly at 4.1(±0.21) hr and 4.6(±0.96) hr, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RbpAR79A doubled at 4.6(±0.96) hr.
source: Whereas RbpAwt doubled at 2.6(±0.16) hr, RbpACD-BL-SID doubled slightly slower at 3.13(±0.16) hr and RbpABL-SID and RbpAR79A doubled even more slowly at 4.1(±0.21) hr and 4.6(±0.96) hr, respectively.
evidence: The claim is supported by growth curve experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: RbpAwt and RbpACD-BL-SID were indistinguishable with regard to cell shape, membrane and nucleoid staining.
source: RbpAwt and RbpACD-BL-SID were indistinguishable with regard to cell shape, membrane and nucleoid staining.
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Cells expressing RbpABL-SID showed an array of morphological changes including filamentous cells, small cells, aberrant membrane staining, nucleoid condensation, and anucleate ghosts.
source: By contrast, cells expressing RbpABL-SID showed an array of morphological changes. These included filamentous cells, small cells, aberrant membrane staining, nucleoid condensation, and anucleate ghosts (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Condensed nucleoids were present in 2.4% of RbpAWT cells.
source: We scored nucleoid morphology as either condensed or diffuse in RbpAWT (n = 208) and RbpABL-SID (n = 248) and observed that condensed nucleoids were present in 2.4% of RbpAWT cells, whereas 25% of RbpABL-SID nucleoids were condensed (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: 25% of RbpABL-SID nucleoids were condensed.
source: We scored nucleoid morphology as either condensed or diffuse in RbpAWT (n = 208) and RbpABL-SID (n = 248) and observed that condensed nucleoids were present in 2.4% of RbpAWT cells, whereas 25% of RbpABL-SID nucleoids were condensed (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claim: RbpAR79A cells did not display morphologic changes compared to WT.
source: RbpAR79A cells, despite their similarly slow growth rate, did not display morphologic changes compared to WT (data not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The essential in vivo function of RbpA can be supplied without the NTT-CD.
source: These findings indicate that, although the essential in vivo function of RbpA can be supplied without the NTT-CD, loss of the CD confers a pleiotropic phenotype of impaired viability and aberrant cell division, likely indicating broad effects on transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the viability of RbpABL-SID expressing cells.

claim: Loss of the CD confers a pleiotropic phenotype of impaired viability and aberrant cell division.
source: These findings indicate that, although the essential in vivo function of RbpA can be supplied without the NTT-CD, loss of the CD confers a pleiotropic phenotype of impaired viability and aberrant cell division, likely indicating broad effects on transcription.
evidence: The claim is supported by in vivo experiments showing growth defects and morphological changes in RbpABL-SID expressing cells.

claim: Loss of the NTT had clear effects on gene expression that were distinct from RbpABL-SID.
source: First, despite the complete complementation by RbpACD-BL-SID for viability, growth, and cell morphology, loss of the NTT had clear effects on gene expression that were distinct from RbpABL-SID, including both overexpressed and underexpressed genes (see red and blue dots, Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The NTT is functional in vivo and may be required for regulation of specific promoters.
source: These results clearly indicate that the NTT is functional in vivo and may be required for regulation of specific promoters.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the distinct gene expression changes observed when the NTT is deleted.

claim: The RbpASID-BL strain had a more globally perturbed pattern of gene expression.
source: The RbpASID-BL strain had an even more globally perturbed pattern of gene expression (Figure 5B–C), consistent with its pleiotropic phenotype (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq experiments shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: There is a core set of genes either up or downregulated by both RbpA alleles.
source: Comparison between the strains indicated a core set of genes either up or downregulated by both RbpA alleles (Figure 5B–C; orange and green points, Supplementary file 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq experiments shown in Figure 5B-C.

claim: The NTT and CD have distinct in vivo transcriptional functions.
source: Taken together, these data define distinct in vivo transcriptional functions for the NTT and CD, as well as a core set of genes that are dysregulated when either the NTT or CD is lost.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the distinct gene expression patterns observed with different RbpA truncations.

claim: The RbpACD interacts with the β'zipper, which interacts with σA3, both of which contact promoter DNA.
source: The RbpACD interacts with the β'zipper, which interacts with σA3, both of which contact promoter DNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The RbpACD interacts with the ZBD, which interacts with σA4, which in turn recognizes the −35 promoter element.
source: The RbpACD also interacts with the ZBD, which interacts with σA4, which in turn recognizes the −35 promoter element.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure and established knowledge of σA4 function.

claim: The RbpASID interacts with σA2, which interacts with the −10 element.
source: The RbpASID interacts with σA2, which interacts with the −10 element.
evidence: The claim is supported by the crystal structure and established knowledge of σA2 function.

claim: RbpA enhances an intricate network of interactions between the ZBD, the zipper, σA2, σA3, σA4, and promoter DNA.
source: Thus, RbpA enhances an intricate network of interactions between the ZBD, the zipper, σA2, σA3, σA4, and promoter DNA.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the structural observations of RbpA interactions with multiple RNAP components.

claim: The fluorescence assay is real-time and relatively non-perturbing.
source: The assay is real-time, relatively non-perturbing (Ko and Heyduk, 2014), and highly versatile; it can be used to study the initiation process on virtually any promoter with any bacterial holo, and can be used to study the mechanistic details of extrinsic factors and small molecules that modulate bacterial transcription initiation, which have been estimated to number in the hundreds (Ishihama, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ko and Heyduk, 2014).

claim: The fluorescence assay can be used to study the initiation process on virtually any promoter with any bacterial holoenzyme.
source: The assay is real-time, relatively non-perturbing (Ko and Heyduk, 2014), and highly versatile; it can be used to study the initiation process on virtually any promoter with any bacterial holo, and can be used to study the mechanistic details of extrinsic factors and small molecules that modulate bacterial transcription initiation, which have been estimated to number in the hundreds (Ishihama, 2000).
evidence: The claim is based on the versatility of the fluorescence assay method.

claim: Extrinsic factors and small molecules that modulate bacterial transcription initiation have been estimated to number in the hundreds.
source: The assay is real-time, relatively non-perturbing (Ko and Heyduk, 2014), and highly versatile; it can be used to study the initiation process on virtually any promoter with any bacterial holo, and can be used to study the mechanistic details of extrinsic factors and small molecules that modulate bacterial transcription initiation, which have been estimated to number in the hundreds (Ishihama, 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Ishihama, 2000).

claim: The −35 element is not important for the formation of RP1.
source: While the −35 element does not appear to be important for the formation of RP1, it is very important for the progression of RP1 to RP2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from kinetic analysis showing no difference in K1 between promoters with and without a -35 element.

claim: The −35 element is very important for the progression of RP1 to RP2.
source: While the −35 element does not appear to be important for the formation of RP1, it is very important for the progression of RP1 to RP2.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis showing large differences in k2 between promoters with and without a -35 element.

claim: The VapB k2 is reduced nearly 50-fold (M. bovis holo) and 230-fold (E. coli holo) compared to AP3.
source: Indeed the most striking kinetic difference between VapB (lacking a −35 element) and AP3 (with a −35 element) is in the RP1 -> RP2 transition (k2, k-2, K2; Supplementary file 6): the VapB k2 is reduced nearly 50-fold (Mbo holo) and 230-fold (Eco holo) compared to AP3.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in Supplementary file 6.

claim: DNA sequence-specific, σ4/−35 element interactions are established as RP2 forms.
source: The simple interpretation of these large effects is that DNA sequence-specific, σ4/−35 element interactions (Campbell et al., 2002) are established as RP2 forms, providing part of the favorable binding free energy to drive the RP1 -> RP2 transition.
evidence: The claim is inferred from kinetic analysis and supported by a citation to published literature (Campbell et al., 2002).

claim: Stabilizing upstream σ4/DNA interactions can stimulate isomerization to RPo.
source: Previous work has shown that stabilizing upstream σ4/DNA interactions can stimulate isomerization to RPo (Dove et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Dove et al., 2000).

claim: Interactions upstream of the −10 element may play a key structural role in facilitating the −11/–12 kink in the DNA by anchoring the lateral position of RNAP on the promoter DNA and/or by constraining the twist of the DNA.
source: Interactions upstream of the −10 element may play a key structural role in facilitating the −11/–12 kink in the DNA (Figure 6) by anchoring the lateral position of RNAP on the promoter DNA and/or by constraining the twist of the DNA.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on structural considerations.

claim: The interaction of RbpA-R79 with the nt-strand −13 phosphate fulfills an anchoring role when σ4/−35 element interactions cannot form.
source: On both AP3 and VapB, RbpA affects only k2, with the largest effect on VapB (Table 1; Supplementary file 8; Figures 3F and 4D), suggesting that the interaction of RbpA-R79 with the nt-strand −13 phosphate (Figure 1B) fulfills this anchoring role when σ4/−35 element interactions cannot form.
evidence: The claim is inferred from kinetic analysis and structural observations.

claim: The majority of M. tuberculosis promoters appear to lack a −35 region.
source: We note the majority of Mtb promoters appear to lack a −35 region (Cortes et al., 2013), suggesting why, in part, RpbA is required for cell viability.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Cortes et al., 2013).

claim: The absence of a −35 region in most M. tuberculosis promoters suggests why RbpA is required for cell viability.
source: We note the majority of Mtb promoters appear to lack a −35 region (Cortes et al., 2013), suggesting why, in part, RpbA is required for cell viability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that RbpA compensates for the lack of -35 elements.

claim: CarD alone stimulates k2 ~10 fold on AP3 with M. bovis holo.
source: In the case of Mbo holo on AP3, CarD alone stimulates k2 ~10 fold.
evidence: The claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: Favorable interactions of the CarD-CTD with promoter DNA require widening of the minor groove at the upstream edge of the −10 element, which is coupled with initial opening of the −10 element and bending of the DNA.
source: Favorable interactions of the CarD-CTD with promoter DNA require widening of the minor groove at the upstream edge of the −10 element (from about −14 to −10), which is coupled with initial opening of the −10 element (Bae et al., 2015a) and bending of the DNA, sending it towards the active site channel (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by structural analysis and a citation to published literature (Bae et al., 2015a).

claim: M. bovis holo on AP3 forms the transcription bubble in a two-stage process, with initial opening of the −10 element in RP2.
source: The 2-AP experiments (Figure 3D–E) indicate that opening of the downstream edge of the transcription bubble does not occur at a rate comparable to the formation of RP2 but at the slower rate of RPo formation. We conclude that Mbo holo on AP3 forms the transcription bubble in a two-stage process, with initial opening of the −10 element in RP2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from 2-AP fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: Further downstream opening creates the transcription bubble in RPo.
source: Further downstream opening then creates the transcription bubble in RPo (Figure 6).
evidence: The claim is inferred from 2-AP fluorescence experiments and kinetic analysis.

claim: A CarD/RbpA protein/protein interaction in the context of the TIC could explain the cooperativity between CarD and RbpA.
source: CarD and RbpA together have a cooperative effect on the RP1 -> RP2 transition, and both factors interact with the promoter DNA at or near the upstream edge of the −10 element (Figures 2D and 6B). A CarD/RbpA protein/protein interaction in the context of the TIC could explain this cooperativity, but this seems unlikely on the basis of the structural modeling (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on structural modeling.

claim: Deletion of the NTT (and the NTT-CD) does not abrogate the CarD/RbpA cooperativity.
source: The RbpANTT is not accounted for in our structure, but deletion of the NTT (and the NTT-CD) does not abrogate the CarD/RbpA cooperativity (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by in vitro transcription assays shown in Figure 2B.

claim: RbpA and CarD affect the same step (RP1 -> RP2 transition), but do so non-competitively and in different ways.
source: Rather, RbpA and CarD affect the same step (RP1 -> RP2 transition), but do so non-competitively and in different ways.
evidence: The claim is inferred from kinetic analysis and structural observations.

claim: Initial opening of the −10 element and DNA bending are coupled.
source: In this scheme, initial opening of the −10 element and DNA bending are coupled.
evidence: The claim is inferred from kinetic and structural analysis.

claim: Through its anchoring role, RbpA stimulates formation of RP2 through facilitating bending, which is coupled with initial opening of the −10 element, facilitating CarD function.
source: Through its anchoring role, RbpA stimulates formation of RP2 through facilitating bending, which is coupled with initial opening of the −10 element, facilitating CarD function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from kinetic and structural analysis.

claim: Through its wedging role, CarD stabilizes the initial −10 opening, which is coupled to bending, facilitating RbpA function.
source: Through its wedging role, CarD stabilizes the initial −10 opening, which is coupled to bending, facilitating RbpA function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from kinetic and structural analysis.

claim: The RP2 -> RPo transition opens the DNA duplex downstream to the start site and loads the t-strand DNA into the RNAP active site.
source: The RP2 -> RPo transition opens the DNA duplex downstream to the start site (Figure 3D) and loads the t-strand DNA into the RNAP active site (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-AP fluorescence experiments and structural models.

claim: The step involving full transcription bubble formation on λPR is rate-limiting in the forward direction, and the same step is rate-limiting in the reverse direction.
source: The step involving full transcription bubble formation on λPR is rate-limiting in the forward direction, and the same step is rate-limiting in the reverse direction (Saecker et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Saecker et al., 2011).

claim: On rrnB P1, stabilization of the full transcription bubble requires ATP and CTP, the first two nucleotides of the transcript.
source: On rrnB P1, stabilization of the full transcription bubble requires ATP and CTP, the first two nucleotides of the transcript (Rutherford et al., 2009), indicating that expansion of the transcription bubble downstream to the start site is energetically difficult in this case as well.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Rutherford et al., 2009).

claim: On AP3, opening of the full transcription bubble occurs during the RP2 -> RPo transition.
source: On AP3, opening of the full transcription bubble occurs during the RP2 -> RPo transition (Figure 3D–E), and this transition is rate-limiting in both directions (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: The claim is supported by 2-AP fluorescence experiments shown in Figure 3D-E.

claim: RbpAR79A supported viability, which was surprising given its loss of function in vitro.
source: In our in vitro analyses, RbpAR79A by itself appeared to have lost all RbpA function in activating transcription and counteracted the activity of CarD when both factors were present (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 8). Therefore, our finding that RbpAR79A supported viability was surprising.
evidence: The claim is based on the contrast between in vitro and in vivo results.

claim: The in vivo role of RbpA is very complex.
source: However, our results clearly show that the in vivo role of RbpA is very complex (Figure 5), and in this work we have only examined two bona fide mycobacterial promoters, AP3 and VapB.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the complex gene expression patterns observed in vivo.

claim: Other promoters are likely regulated by RbpAR79A in vivo, possibly through the action of additional conserved basic residues on the BL such as K76.
source: It seems likely that other promoters are regulated by RbpAR79Ain vivo, possibly through the action of additional conserved basic residues on the BL such as K76 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the viability of RbpAR79A expressing cells and the presence of other conserved basic residues.

claim: RbpA-R79 interaction with duplex DNA upstream of the −10 provides an anchoring role that facilitates the bending (RP2) and subsequent formation of the full transcription bubble (RPo).
source: With our in vitro functional analysis and in combination with our previous analyses of CarD structure and function (Bae et al., 2015a; Davis et al., 2015; Srivastava et al., 2013), we propose the following model (Figure 6B): RbpA-R79 interaction with duplex DNA upstream of the −10 provides an anchoring role that facilitates the bending (RP2) and subsequent formation of the full transcription bubble (RPo).
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on in vitro functional analysis and structural data.

claim: Initial distortions of the DNA in RP2 are compatible with CarD to wedge its conserved Trp residue into the splayed minor groove.
source: Initial distortions of the DNA in RP2 are compatible with CarD to wedge its conserved Trp residue into the splayed minor groove, which not only contributes to formation of the RP2 intermediate, but also serves as a barrier for bubble collapse once RPo has formed.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on structural and functional data.

claim: CarD wedging serves as a barrier for bubble collapse once RPo has formed.
source: Initial distortions of the DNA in RP2 are compatible with CarD to wedge its conserved Trp residue into the splayed minor groove, which not only contributes to formation of the RP2 intermediate, but also serves as a barrier for bubble collapse once RPo has formed.
evidence: The claim is a proposed model based on structural and functional data.

claim: The role of RbpA in facilitating the formation of RP2 is particularly important at promoters lacking sequence elements upstream of the −10 element.
source: The role of RbpA in facilitating the formation of RP2 is particularly important at promoters lacking sequence elements upstream of the −10 element, which represents the majority of Mtb promoters (Cortes et al., 2013), possibly explaining why RbpA is essential and spotlighting the importance of studying a diversity of organisms in efforts to characterize 'conserved' processes such as transcription.
evidence: The claim is inferred from kinetic analysis and supported by a citation to published literature (Cortes et al., 2013).
